title: Frogs, Gnats, and Flies: The Finger of God
summary: Three more plagues fall on Egypt. Frogs swarm out of the Nile into houses, beds, and ovens; the dust of the land becomes gnats; and thick swarms of flies ruin the country, though not the land of Goshen where Israel lives. Pharaoh begins to bargain, asking Moses to pray and offering partial permission, but each time relief comes he hardens his heart again, even after his own magicians admit, “This is the finger of God.”
story: The contest that began with the Nile turning to blood intensifies. Chapter 8 completes the first group of three plagues and opens the second, and two new things happen. The magicians, who matched the first two signs, fail at the third and confess that a power beyond theirs is at work. Then, with the flies, God begins to separate Israel from Egypt, so that the plagues fall on one people and pass over the other, a pattern that will reach its climax on the night of the Passover. Pharaoh, for his part, starts to negotiate. He never quite says no, and he never truly says yes, and the chapter shows how a hard heart bargains.
historical:
Goshen, where Jacob's family settled (Genesis 45:10), lay in the eastern Nile Delta, and many scholars locate it around the Wadi Tumilat, a valley running east from the Delta toward the Sinai frontier, suitable for grazing flocks. From the fourth plague on, the text insists that the land of Goshen was spared (verse 22), and chapter 9 repeats the point for the livestock and the hail. This matters to the story's claim. The plagues are not simply disasters that happen to strike Egypt; they discriminate between peoples living side by side.

Pharaoh's offers also reflect the realities of power. He first asks for prayer and promises release (verse 8), then allows sacrifice inside Egypt (verse 25), then outside it but not far away (verse 28). Each offer keeps the slaves within reach. Moses' reply in verse 26 explains why worship could not happen in Egypt: Israel's sacrifices would be detestable to the Egyptians. Genesis already notes that Egyptians would not eat with Hebrews (Genesis 43:32) and that shepherds were detestable to them (Genesis 46:34). Some interpreters add that certain animals, such as the Apis bull and rams linked with the god Amun, were sacred in Egypt, so that sacrificing such animals openly could provoke violence, which is exactly what Moses fears: “will they not stone us?”
cultural:
Frogs multiplied in Egypt as the Nile's floodwaters went down, and they had a place in religion as well as nature. The goddess Heqet, a figure associated with birth and fertility, was pictured as a frog or with a frog's head. A land overrun by frogs, in its bedrooms, ovens, and kneading bowls, was fertility turned into a curse, and the frogs that die in stinking heaps (verse 14) make even the relief unbearable. The creatures of the third and fourth plagues are harder to identify. The word for gnats may mean lice, gnats, or mosquitoes. The word for the fourth plague means a swarm or mixture; the ancient Greek translation took it as a biting dog-fly, while some Jewish interpreters understood a mixture of wild animals. The BSB, like most English versions, reads flies.

When Moses tells Pharaoh “You may have the honor over me” (verse 9), he is using a courtly idiom that lets Pharaoh name the time. The point is to rule out coincidence: if the frogs leave exactly when Pharaoh chooses, he will know “that there is no one like the LORD our God” (verse 10). Pharaoh's answer, “Tomorrow,” means one more night with the frogs, a touch of dark humor in the telling.
literary: Readers comparing translations should know that the verse numbers differ here. English Bibles, including the BSB, begin chapter 8 four verses earlier than the Hebrew text, so English 8:1-4 is Hebrew 7:26-29 and English 8:5-32 is Hebrew 8:1-28. The chapter follows the three-part pattern of the plague cycle: the frogs are announced after Moses goes in to Pharaoh (verse 1), the gnats come without warning (verse 16), and the flies begin a new group of three with a morning meeting at the water (verse 20). The magicians' role builds to a turning point. They copy the frogs (verse 7), fail at the gnats (verse 18), and then vanish from the contest until the boils. Pharaoh's responses escalate in a different way. For the first time he asks for prayer, promises release, and names terms, and for the first time the text says that Pharaoh himself hardened his heart (verses 15 and 32), using the verb for making heavy. The phrase “just as the LORD had said” closes the frogs and the gnats, keeping the reader aware that nothing here surprises God.

outline.t: Pharaoh asks for prayer, then hardens his heart
The third plague: gnats, and the finger of God
The fourth plague: swarms of flies, and Goshen spared
Pharaoh bargains, Moses prays, and Pharaoh hardens again

doctrines.note: God says the plague on Egypt but not Goshen will show “that I, the LORD, am in the land” (verse 22). The God of a slave people is not confined to their territory; he rules in the heart of Egypt, over its river, dust, and insects.

Twice Pharaoh asks Moses to pray, and twice Moses does, and God does “as Moses requested” (verses 13 and 31). Moses intercedes for the man oppressing his people, and God hears, even knowing that Pharaoh will harden his heart again.

Beginning with the flies, God puts a distinction between his people and Egypt. Salvation in Exodus is not only rescue from suffering but being set apart by God, marked as his own while judgment falls around them.

words.note: Etsba, finger. When the magicians say “This is the finger of God” (verse 19), they concede that a power beyond their arts is at work, though they may mean a god rather than Israel's God in particular. The phrase returns when the tablets of the law are written “by the finger of God” (31:18), and Jesus uses it of his own power over demons (Luke 11:20).

Pedut, redemption or ransom. In verse 23 the Hebrew literally says God will put a redemption between his people and Egypt's. The BSB, following the ancient Greek translation and most modern versions, renders distinction, and some scholars think the text originally used a similar word meaning separation. Either way, the separation God makes is the beginning of Israel's redemption.

To'evah, something detestable or abhorrent, often translated abomination. It names what offends someone's religious or moral sense. Moses uses it in verse 26 of how Israel's sacrifices would look to Egyptians; elsewhere in the law it names what is detestable to the LORD, such as idolatry and injustice. What is sacred to one people can be abhorrent to another, which is why Israel had to go out to worship.

Atar, to pray or plead. It is used only of prayer to God, and here it appears five times as Pharaoh asks for prayer and Moses offers it. The king who asked “Who is the LORD?” in 5:2 now asks Moses to plead with him, which is progress of a kind, though not yet repentance.

christ: Jesus picked up the magicians' words. Accused of casting out demons by the power of Satan, he answered, “But if I drive out demons by the finger of God, then the kingdom of God has come upon you” (Luke 11:20). Matthew's version of the same saying has “the Spirit of God” (Matthew 12:28). Jesus is claiming that the power the Egyptian experts could not match, the power that humbled Pharaoh, is at work in his own ministry, and that a greater exodus has begun, a release of captives from a darker master. The chapter also shows Moses praying for his oppressor, which anticipates the teaching of Jesus, “love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you” (Matthew 5:44). And the distinction God makes between his people and Egypt points forward to the Passover and beyond it to the church, which Peter calls “a people for God’s own possession” (1 Peter 2:9). These links are thematic rather than predictive, but they belong to the same story of God setting apart a people for himself.

hard.q: Can the plagues be explained as natural events, and if so, are they still miracles?
hard.a:
Since the nineteenth century, many readers have noticed that the first plagues look like a chain reaction. The best known version was worked out by the scholar Greta Hort in the late 1950s. On this view an unusually high Nile flood, carrying red earth and microorganisms, turned the river red and killed the fish; frogs fled the fouled water and died; insects bred in the rotting heaps; disease spread by insects struck the livestock and caused skin sores; and the later hail, locusts, and darkness (perhaps a severe sandstorm) belong to the Egyptian seasons that follow. Others reject such accounts as missing what the text claims, a series of direct acts of God with no natural mechanism.

Many interpreters take a middle position. The Bible itself names natural means for some of God's acts, such as the east wind that brings the locusts (10:13) and drives back the sea (14:21), so natural causes and divine action are not opposites in Scripture. What makes the plagues signs, on this view, is not the absence of nature but their intensity, their timing, and their precision: each is announced beforehand, begins and ends at Moses' word (Pharaoh even picks the hour in verse 10), and from the fourth plague on spares Goshen while striking the rest of Egypt. On any of these readings the text's claim is the same: the God of Israel controls the powers that Egypt feared and worshiped.

questions: Pharaoh asks for relief but not for change, and when relief comes he hardens his heart. Where do you see that pattern in your own prayers or promises?
Moses prays sincerely for the man oppressing his people. What would it look like for you to pray for someone who has harmed you or those you love?
The magicians recognized “the finger of God” before Pharaoh did. Why do people sometimes see the truth and still refuse to act on it?
